ex abundantia — “out of abundance”; “from an overflow.”

Just — Arthur W. Just, “Russische Gegenwart.” In: Europäische Revue 8, 1932, pp. 94–103; also by the same author, “Russische Gegenwart. Der zweite Fünfjahresplan.” In: Europäische Revue 8, 1932, pp. 303–313.

Karl Renner — (1870–1950), Austrian lawyer and politician. Schmitt is referring to K. Renner, “Die soziale Funktion der Rechtsinstitute.” In: Marx-Studien 1, 1904, pp. 65–192; later also published several times as a separate work.
“easy prey to the power of the moment” — “Man, living and feeling, is easy prey to the power of the moment.” Friedrich Schiller, The Maid of Orleans, III, 4.
Yes, he fishes for pearls … — From the poem “Der Dichter – Dichters Glück” by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff.

Gustav Klemm — Gustav Friedrich Klemm (1802–1867), cultural historian and librarian. He regarded inequality among human races as the driving force of world history, an idea later taken up by German nationalist and racialist circles. Klemm’s principal work is the ten-volume Allgemeine Culturgeschichte der Menschheit.

Fauchille — Paul Auguste Joseph Fauchille (1858–1926), French lawyer. Schmitt is referring to Paul Fauchille, Traité de droit international public, 8th edition, completely revised, expanded, and brought up to date from Henry Bonfils’s Manuel de droit international public, Vols. I.1–3 and II, Paris, 1922–1926. See also Nomos, p. 235, n. 2.

Verdross — This refers to Alfred Verdross’s article “Amnestie” in Karl Strupp, ed., Wörterbuch des Völkerrechts und der Diplomatie. Begonnen von Julius Hatschek. Fortges. und hrsg. von Karl Strupp, Vols. 1–3, Berlin and elsewhere, 1924–1929. See also Nomos, p. 235, n. 2.
Grotius III 10, §§ 3–4 — Schmitt is referring to Hugo Grotius, De jure belli ac pacis libri tres.

Gudelin: in amnestia … — “The substance of peace consists in amnesty; without it, there is no peace.” Schmitt took this quotation from the lawyer Peter Gudelin (1550–1619) from the following book: Heinrich Rogge, Nationale Friedenspolitik. Handbuch des Friedensproblems und seiner Wissenschaft auf der Grundlage systematischer Völkerrechtspolitik, Berlin, 1934, p. 55. Ernst Forsthoff drew Schmitt’s attention to the passage on 17 October 1951; cf. BW Forsthoff, p. 80.

Art. 120 of the Jacobin Constitution of 1793 — The article reads in the original: “It gives asylum to foreigners banished from their homeland for the cause of liberty. — It refuses asylum to tyrants.”
JW 1933 — Hans Kasche, “Das politische Verbrechen in den deutschen Auslieferungsverträgen.” In: Juristische Wochenschrift, issues 29/30, 62nd year (1933), pp. 1639–1640.
Lauterpacht — Lassa Oppenheim, Disputes, War and Neutrality, Part 2 of International Law, edited by Hersch Lauterpacht, 6th ed., London and elsewhere, 1940.

Itinerarium acroamaticum … — “An entertaining guide to the roads of hell. A book of instruction on how, through proper conduct of one’s life, to keep out of Leviathan’s way.” Probably inspired by Theodor Däubler, Lucidarium in arte musicae des Ricciotto Canudo aus Gioja del Colle, Hellerau, 1917.
De nobis ipsis silemus — See the note above on p. 83.
I already know those dear Germans — See the note above on p. 129.
exul in patria — See the note above on p. 7.
inuar uigandun — From the Merseburg Incantations:
Break free from the bonds, escape from the enemies.
I endure, watchful … — A line written in 1908 by Schmitt’s friend Franz Kluxen. Schmitt wrote it down from memory in 1948 together with several other lines by Kluxen; cf. RW 265, no. 21288.
Gelimer’s laughter — See the note above on p. 312.

Durando saecula vincit — Multa virum volvens durando saecula vincit. “After passing through many generations of men, it conquers the centuries by enduring.” Publius Vergilius Maro, Georgics, Book II, line 295; German translation by Johann Heinrich Voß.
Quo usque tandem? — Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra? “How much longer, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?” Marcus Tullius Cicero, First Catilinarian Oration.
